title: Coset basis and finite presentation for subgroup group algebras
statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $M$ an additive abelian group, and $L\subseteq M$ a subgroup. Use the group algebras of [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group], so $R[M]$ is the free $R$-module on $e_m$ with $e_me_n=e_{m+n}$. The inclusion $j:R[L]\to R[M]$, $e_l\mapsto e_l$, is injective. For any representatives $t_c\in M$ of the cosets $c\in M/L$, the elements $(e_{t_c})_{c\in M/L}$ are an $R[L]$-basis of $R[M]$ [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. Suppose $M/L$ is finitely generated. Choose a decomposition $M/L\cong\mathbf Z^r\oplus\bigoplus_{j=1}^s\mathbf Z/d_j\mathbf Z$ with $r,s\geq0$ and $d_j\geq2$, lifts $a_i,b_j\in M$ of the indicated free and cyclic generators, and put $l_j=d_jb_j\in L$. Then the homomorphism
$$R[L][X_1^{\pm1},\ldots,X_r^{\pm1},Y_1^{\pm1},\ldots,Y_s^{\pm1}]/(Y_j^{d_j}-e_{l_j}:1\leq j\leq s)\longrightarrow R[M],\quad X_i\longmapsto e_{a_i},\ Y_j\longmapsto e_{b_j},$$
which is $j$ on coefficients, is an isomorphism. Here a Laurent polynomial ring means finite sums of monomials with integer exponents, and adjoining $Z^{\pm1}$ means adjoining $Z,W$ subject to $ZW=1$. In particular $R[M]$ is a finitely presented $R[L]$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-finitely-presented-algebra]. The displayed homomorphism remains an isomorphism after any homomorphism of base rings $R\to R'$, with every $e_m$ sent to the same indexed basis element. The zero ring, $L=M$, $L=0$, and torsion in $M$ are allowed.

source.place: Theorem 12.9(b), printed pp.233-234, group-algebra injection and quotient calculation; relative algebra strengthening and explicit coset/Laurent normal form written by Q96. proof.text: Put $A=R[L]$. The finitely supported map $j$ sends $\sum_{l\in L}r_le_l$ to the same sum indexed by the distinct elements $l\in M$. The coefficient of $e_l$ in its image is $r_l$, so its kernel is zero. It respects multiplication because $e_{l+l\prime}=e_le_{l\prime}$, and sends the unit $e_0$ to $e_0$. Thus it gives the specified injective ring map and the $A$-algebra structure on $R[M]$.

source.place: Theorem 12.9(b), printed pp.233-234; agent relative-ring strengthening: explicit coset and Laurent normal forms.

proof.text: For any chosen representatives, the function $L\times(M/L)\to M$, $(l,c)\mapsto l+t_c$, is a bijection: for $m\in M$ its inverse is $(m-t_{\bar m},\bar m)$. Consequently regrouping a finite sum by $c$ gives $\sum_mr_me_m=\sum_c(\sum_lr_{l+t_c}e_l)e_{t_c}$. Its coefficients in $A$ are unique, since equality of two such sums gives equality at each $e_{l+t_c}$. This is exactly the asserted $A$-basis, with no finiteness restriction on $M/L$.

source.place: Theorem 12.9(b), printed pp.233-234; agent relative-ring strengthening: explicit coset and Laurent normal forms.

proof.text: When $M/L$ is finitely generated, apply the cited abelian-group structure theorem to $M/L$. Delete factors with exponent zero, whose cyclic group is $\mathbf Z/1\mathbf Z=0$, and enumerate the remaining finite index set. Finite-support functions on a finite set are ordinary tuples. This gives a decomposition of the stated form with $d_j\geq2$. The argument below works for any such chosen decomposition, not only the prime-power decomposition furnished by the theorem. Lift its generators along $M\twoheadrightarrow M/L$. Then $l_j=d_jb_j\in L$, and the elements $t_{n,q}=\sum_i n_ia_i+\sum_jq_jb_j$, where $n\in\mathbf Z^r$ and $0\leq q_j<d_j$, are exactly one representative per coset.

source.place: AddCommGroup.equiv_free_prod_directSum_zmod, lines 119-132; elementary deletion of trivial cyclic summands.

proof.text: First handle $R=0$: all the rings in the presentation are zero rings, their underlying modules have unique coefficient families, and all asserted maps are the unique isomorphisms. Henceforth suppose $R\ne0$. Set $B=A[X_1^{\pm1},\ldots,X_r^{\pm1}]$, $C_0=B$ and $C_j=C_{j-1}[Y_j]/(Y_j^{d_j}-e_{l_j})$. In each step the polynomial is monic of degree $d_j$, so the cited monic-quotient basis gives a unique expression $\sum_{q_j<d_j}c_{q_j}y_j^{q_j}$ over $C_{j-1}$. Induction starting at $C_0=B$ therefore gives a unique expression $\sum_q c_qy_1^{q_1}\cdots y_s^{q_s}$ in $C_s$ with $c_q\in B$. The coefficient rings remain nonzero: the power-basis expression of a nonzero constant cannot be zero. Expanding each $c_q$ into its finite Laurent sum shows that $C_s$ has $A$-basis $X^ny^q$, with $n\in\mathbf Z^r$ and $0\leq q_j<d_j$.

source.place: Tag 04GG (lemma-characterize-henselian), monic-quotient freeness used in its proof; power-basis form in AdjoinRoot.powerBasis', Mathlib/RingTheory/AdjoinRoot.lean:633; finite iteration and Laurent expansion written here.

proof.text: Let $P$ denote the Laurent quotient displayed in the statement. In $C_s$ the element $e_{l_j}$ is a unit with inverse $e_{-l_j}$, and $y_j^{-1}=e_{-l_j}y_j^{d_j-1}$, since their product is $e_{-l_j}y_j^{d_j}=1$. Evaluating Laurent monomials at these units defines $P\to C_s$. Conversely the successive polynomial-quotient maps sending $y_j$ to the class of $Y_j$ define $C_s\to P$. Both composites fix coefficients, all $X_i^{\pm1}$, and all $y_j$ or $Y_j^{\pm1}$, respectively, so they are identity maps on all finite monomial sums. This identifies $P$ with $C_s$ and its basis with the monomials $X^nY^q$ of the preceding step.

source.place: Theorem 12.9(b), printed pp.233-234; agent relative-ring strengthening: explicit coset and Laurent normal forms.

proof.text: Each $e_{a_i}$ and $e_{b_j}$ is a unit, with inverse given by negating its index, and $(e_{b_j})^{d_j}=e_{l_j}$. Thus evaluation defines the displayed $A$-algebra homomorphism $P\to R[M]$. It sends $X^nY^q$ to $e_{t_{n,q}}$. Step 3 says that these $t_{n,q}$ are coset representatives; Step 2 says their images are an $A$-basis of $R[M]$. Together with Steps 4-5 this proves bijectivity: expand an element uniquely in the respective basis, and keep the same coefficients in the other basis to obtain the inverse. A bijective algebra homomorphism is an algebra isomorphism, as applying the homomorphism to both sides of each algebra law verifies that its inverse preserves that law.

source.place: Theorem 12.9(b), printed pp.233-234; agent relative-ring strengthening: explicit coset and Laurent normal forms.

proof.text: Replace the $r+s$ Laurent variables by pairs of ordinary polynomial variables $X_i,U_i$ and $Y_j,V_j$, with relations $X_iU_i-1$, $Y_jV_j-1$, and $Y_j^{d_j}-e_{l_j}$. The map to $P$ sends $U_i$ to $X_i^{-1}$ and $V_j$ to $Y_j^{-1}$. The inverse sends every negative power to the corresponding power of $U_i$ or $V_j$; the product-one relations make these assignments inverse. This is a presentation with $2(r+s)$ variables and $r+2s$ relations over $A$, so the definition of finite presentation applies. For $r=s=0$ it is the presentation $A\cong A$ with no variables or relations.

source.place: Theorem 12.9(b), printed pp.233-234; agent relative-ring strengthening: explicit coset and Laurent normal forms.

proof.text: For any ring homomorphism $f:R\to R\prime$, the coefficient map on group algebras is $\sum_mr_me_m\mapsto\sum_mf(r_m)e_m$; on Laurent polynomials apply $f$ to each coefficient in $A=R[L]$ and fix the variables. It sends every relation $Y_j^{d_j}-e_{l_j}$ to the identically indexed relation over $R\prime$, and commutes with evaluation on coefficients and on every variable and inverse variable. The same coset decomposition, unit formula and normal forms in Steps 1-7 over $R\prime$ prove that the resulting displayed map is an isomorphism, including when $R\prime=0$. Its inverse likewise keeps the indices $t_{n,q}$ and applies $f$ only to coefficients. Thus the isomorphism has exactly the stated compatibility with every base-ring homomorphism. No torsion element was cancelled and no integer $d_j$ was inverted anywhere.
